contentBlocks.text: The Origin of the Toyota Name: From "Toyoda" to "Toyota"
The Toyota brand takes its name from founder Kiichiro Toyoda. But the company wasn’t always called Toyota. When its automotive division first launched in 1933, it used the family name: Toyoda.

In July 1936, the company held a public logo contest to mark its first passenger car and build visibility. Out of 27,000 submissions, a circular design featuring the Japanese characters for “Toyota” (トヨタ) won.
That winning design led the company to fully rebrand around the name Toyota. On August 28, 1937, Toyota Motor Company was officially founded, making the switch from the family name official.
Why the Change?
Moving from Toyoda to Toyota wasn’t random—it was a deliberate choice. Here’s why the new name worked better for the brand:

Aesthetics and Sound: The Japanese characters for Toyota look cleaner and more modern. The name also sounds lighter and clearer in Japanese, using softer voiceless sounds that feel smoother than the sharper, voiced tones in Toyoda.

The "Lucky 8": In Japanese culture, eight is a lucky number tied to growth and success. Toyota (トヨタ) is written in exactly eight brush strokes, making it a natural fit for a brand with big global plans.
Modern Branding: Toyoda literally means “fertile rice paddies.” The new name helped the company move past its farming-related roots and project a more modern image.
A New Corporate Identity: The shift showed how much the company had evolved. No longer just a small family operation, it was positioning itself to become a major global player.

In short, the change from Toyoda to Toyota was far more than a small spelling tweak. It marked a defining rebranding moment that turned a family loom business into one of the world’s largest automakers.
Brand Profile
What Does the Toyota Logo Mean?

It’s a sight you see every single day on the road, yet most people don’t know the real story behind Toyota’s three-oval emblem. Launched in 1989 to mark the brand’s 50th anniversary, every curve of this iconic mark has a purpose.
The large outer oval represents the world—it reflects Toyota’s global presence and its goal to serve drivers everywhere.

Inside, two ovals overlap to create a stylized T for Toyota. One oval symbolizes the customer’s heart, while the other stands for the company’s heart. Their connection shows trust between them. The combined shape also looks like a steering wheel, reminding us of the driving experience.

The lines, which resemble uneven brushstrokes, are inspired by traditional Japanese calligraphy. This gives the logo a simple and unique look that’s easy to recognize from the front or even in a rearview mirror.
All the open space around the ovals stands for infinite values Toyota stands for: solid quality, everyday reliability, driving joy, and constant innovation.
Toyota Logo Timeline
This is Toyota’s very first official logo, dating all the way back to 1935.

Before it became a global automotive giant, Toyota started as an automotive division within Toyota Automatic Loom Works. This badge was the company’s first trademark, registered in July 1935 for its early vehicles.
The design is simple: a blue octagon with “TOYODA” across the middle, taking its name from the founding family’s actual last name.
This logo appeared on Toyota’s first production models, including the AA, AB, AC sedans and G1 trucks. All of these were built before the company officially became Toyota Motor Corporation in 1937.

This badge is more than just an old symbol. It represents a key part of Toyota’s early history, showing how the brand began as part of a loom business before growing into one of the largest automakers in the world.

In 1936, Toyoda Automatic Loom Works held a public logo contest for its car division. They were looking for a design to help promote their vehicles, and picked a winner from more than 27,000 entries. The winning logo was a circular design with the Japanese characters “トヨタ” (Toyota).
The company changed its name from Toyoda to Toyota in 1937. The new name was easier to say and remember, and it also used eight brush strokes in Japanese — a lucky number in Japanese culture.
The 1936 logo contest ended up being a big step in building the Toyota brand we know today.

The 1958 Toyota logo was a big change from the company’s earlier emblems. Toyota moved away from geometric shapes and used English lettering for the first time. The result was a straightforward badge: the word “Toyota” in black on a white background, with uneven stroke weights and thin, sharp serifs at the ends of the letters.
The bold, serif font felt clean but refined, somewhat similar to typefaces like Times New Roman. Its simple, timeless look made the logo easy to recognize and remember, so it stayed in use for years.
This design helped Toyota build a recognizable brand identity in the American market, and it went on to become the foundation for the company’s modern wordmark.

In 1969, Toyota gave its logo a more modern update. The old serif style was gone, replaced with a clean, black sans-serif wordmark. The letters were tight and compact, using a straightforward geometric font with sharp, simple lines and no extra frills.

It didn’t look all that different from the old logo, but it felt a lot sleeker. The letters were packed close together, with the Y fitting right between the two O’s — giving it a tight, balanced look that felt more up-to-date for the time.
In 1978, Toyota changed its logo again, bringing back the bright red-and-white color scheme. The wordmark here already looks a lot like the one the brand uses today.
The font was similar to the earlier version, but a bit shorter and with more space between the letters. That probably made the whole logo easier to read and just nicer to look at.
This design really laid the groundwork for the classic Toyota logo we all know now.

Toyota unveiled its now-famous three-oval emblem in October 1989, celebrating the brand’s 50th anniversary. The design has stayed remarkably consistent over the years, with only small updates to the font and coloring.
The logo is made up of three overlapping ovals. The two inner ovals stand for the bond between Toyota and its customers, and together they form a subtle “T” in the center.
The outer oval wraps around the whole design, representing Toyota’s global presence and its ongoing ambition to grow and innovate around the world.

In 2005, Toyota changed its logo in a few important ways. They moved the red emblem above the “TOYOTA” lettering and gave it a 3D effect with a silver gradient. The badge was also made bigger, and its edges thicker, which made it stand out more and feel more dynamic. The lettering didn’t change much, just a darker, deeper shade of red than before.
This new logo quickly became closely associated with Toyota, especially since it appeared on the hood of most of their cars. It remains one of the brand’s most recognizable logo designs.
Since Toyota rolled out its new look in 2019, the company has pretty much retired the 3D logo for all its brand communications.

While the core design has stayed the same, you’ll still see different versions popping up in certain markets or for specific campaigns. These small tweaks are really about helping the brand vibe better with local cultures and fit into regional marketing plans.

Take the U.S. market, for example: the logo features that classic white three-oval symbol inside a bright red square, with "Toyota" written to the right in a clean, black sans-serif font. There are a few other stylized versions out there, too, depending on where you look.

By 2020, like a lot of big tech and car companies, Toyota switched over to a flat design style. It got rid of that 3D chrome finish for good, using a clean, simple 2D emblem instead. The whole look feels a lot more modern and built for screens, looking good on anything from small phone displays to huge billboards.

Probably the most noticeable change is that in quite a few markets, Toyota stopped using its name next to the logo altogether. The three-oval emblem is so well-known that the brand lets it speak for itself now. Most of the time, it shows up as a basic black icon on a white background, or the other way around. It’s a simple, confident choice — the company doesn’t have to write its name out anymore, because people know exactly who it is just from those ovals.
